title: Anatomy of Proof
subtitle: Five moments that taught the law to hear the body

quests.title: The First Autopsy
quests.scene: Fort St. George, Madras. August 28, 1693. James Wheeler — a member of the Madras Council — is dead. He was treated by Dr. Samuel Browne, whose assistant ground pearls in a pestle and mortar previously used for arsenic. The town suspects poisoning. The law has no way to prove it.
quests.question: You are Dr. Edward Bulkley. The court has no procedure for this. Do you open the body to find the truth?

choices.text: Trust the suspicion — let the case go to trial
choices.outcome: Browne would have been convicted on suspicion alone. Innocent or guilty, the law would have made a guess.

choices.text: Walk away — this is not a physician's business
choices.outcome: The case would have been decided by rumor. Justice would have been blind.

choices.text: Open the body and let it speak
choices.outcome: You performed the first complete medico-legal autopsy in India. The body told you there was no arsenic. Browne was acquitted.

quests.outcome: Bulkley opens the body. No arsenic found. Samuel Browne is acquitted.
quests.whatChanged: The body becomes a legal witness. Forensic medicine in India begins on a hot August day in Madras, 1693.
quests.whoBuiltOnThis: Bulkley could only see. For 143 years, that's all a physician could do — look at the body and describe what he saw. It would take another invention to prove what the eye could not see.

quests.title: The Invisible Crime
quests.scene: London, 1836. Arsenic poisoning is the perfect crime — invisible, tasteless, and almost impossible to prove. Courts convict on suspicion or not at all. A chemist named James Marsh is called to testify in a poisoning case. He can describe the symptoms, but he cannot prove the poison was there.
quests.question: You are James Marsh. You know arsenic is present. You cannot prove it to a jury. What do you do?

choices.outcome: The jury would weigh your word against the defense's denial — exactly the state of forensic medicine for 143 years.

choices.text: Give up — chemistry can't help here
choices.outcome: Poisoners would continue to walk free. The perfect crime would remain perfect.

choices.text: Find a way to make arsenic visible
choices.outcome: You develop the Marsh Test — mixing the suspected sample with hydrogen gas, which produces a mirror-like deposit of arsenic on cold glass. A tiny amount becomes unmistakable.

quests.outcome: Marsh invents a test that turns invisible arsenic into a visible mirror on glass. Poison becomes provable.
quests.whatChanged: Forensic medicine gains its first chemical tool. The invisible becomes visible.
quests.whoBuiltOnThis: The Marsh Test could detect arsenic. But a test in a lab is not the same as evidence in a courtroom. Someone had to bridge the two — a toxicologist willing to testify.

quests.title: The Chemist in the Courtroom
quests.scene: Paris, 1840. The Lafarge trial — a widow accused of poisoning her husband with arsenic. The prosecution has the Marsh Test. The defense has skeptics who say the test proves nothing. The courtroom has never seen a chemist testify as an authority before.
quests.question: You are Mathieu Orfila. You have the test results. Do you testify?

choices.text: Present the evidence and let the jury decide
choices.outcome: You explain the Marsh Test step by step — what it detects, how reliable it is, what the results mean. The jury convicts. Forensic toxicology enters the courtroom for the first time.

choices.text: Decline — chemists shouldn't testify in court
choices.outcome: The test exists, but no one can explain it to a jury. Poisoners still walk free. The Marsh Test sits in a lab, unused.
A written report carries less weight than a spoken expert. The jury remains uncertain. The case is undecided.

quests.outcome: Orfila testifies. Lafarge is convicted. Forensic toxicology enters the courtroom.
quests.whatChanged: Poison is no longer a matter of suspicion. It can be proven, and the proof can be trusted by a jury.
quests.whoBuiltOnThis: Chemistry could now prove what happened. But the next question was who did it. Proving identity — the fingerprint — would be the next revolution.

quests.title: The Body's Signature
quests.scene: Calcutta, 1858. William Herschel begins fingerprinting locals as a form of signature. Thirty-nine years later, in London, Edward Richard Henry turns the idea into a system — a classification method that any police officer can use. Fingerprints are unique, permanent, and impossible to forge. The question is whether the law will accept them.
quests.question: You are Edward Richard Henry. Herschel proved fingerprints work. Now you must make them usable — for every crime scene, every officer, every court.

choices.outcome: Identity remains unprovable. Criminal records stay unreliable. The same person can be arrested twice under different names.
Body measurements work in theory but fail in practice. Two measurements can match by accident. The method is eventually abandoned.

choices.text: Build a classification system for fingerprints
choices.outcome: You create the Henry Classification System — a way to file, search, and match fingerprints at scale. Scotland Yard adopts it in 1901. The method spreads worldwide.

quests.outcome: Henry creates the classification system. Fingerprints become the first globally adopted forensic identification technique.
quests.whatChanged: The body becomes evidence of identity. Every crime scene now has the potential to name a suspect — and the method started in India.
quests.whoBuiltOnThis: Fingerprints prove identity. But every other trace a criminal leaves — a hair, a fiber, a fleck of paint — was still invisible to the law. It would take another century to make them visible.

quests.title: The Survivor's Turn
quests.scene: Delhi, December 2012. A young woman is assaulted on a bus. She dies. The country erupts in protest. The law has historically treated the survivor as evidence — her body examined, questioned, doubted. The Justice Verma Committee is formed to rewrite the framework.
quests.question: You are Justice J.S. Verma. Do you reform the procedure, or transform its purpose?

choices.outcome: The framework remains — but the survivor is still examined, still doubted, still treated as evidence.
Punishment increases, but the process of examination remains the same. The survivor still testifies through her body, in a system designed for the accused.

choices.text: Rewrite the framework around survivor care
choices.outcome: The Committee recommends sweeping reforms. The Criminal Law Amendment Act 2013 enacts them. The MoHFW 2014 Guidelines follow — survivor-centered care, informed consent, and the ban on the two-finger test.

quests.outcome: The Committee recommends sweeping reforms. Parliament enacts the Criminal Law Amendment Act 2013. The MoHFW 2014 Guidelines follow.
quests.whatChanged: The law shifts from evidence-collection to survivor care. The two-finger test is banned. The framework prioritizes dignity, consent, and recovery.
quests.whoBuiltOnThis: The 2013 Amendment and the BNSS 2023 are the current framework. The quest ends here. But the story continues with every case that follows.
